docs.title: Artificial intelligence applications in histopathology
docs.text: Cagla Deniz Bahadir, Mohamed Omar, Jacob Rosenthal et al. · 2024 · Nature Reviews Electrical Engineering doi · paper

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Bahadir et al. is a broad survey of the deep-learning toolkit applied to histopathology, written from the perspective of the electrical-engineering and machine-learning community developing the underlying techniques. The author list spans computational (Bahadir, Sabuncu — Cornell ECE) and clinical (Liechty, Pisapia — Weill Cornell pathology) ends of the pipeline, giving the review a useful pragmatic flavour.

With ~206 references, it covers most of the modern pathology AI stack:

  • WSI acquisition and preprocessing — slide formats, tissue masking, stain normalisation.
  • Deep-learning architectures — CNNs, ViTs, graph neural networks, transformer MIL.
  • Weakly-supervised MIL — ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning, CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL, TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL, DSMIL, DTFD-MIL, and the Campanella et al. 2019 — Clinical-Grade Weakly-Supervised Pathology MIL clinical-grade scale demonstration.
  • Pathology foundation models — patch-level SSL (CTransPath (Swin-T, SRCL), UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2)-era) and the vision-only PFM cohort.
  • Vision-language pretraining — CLIP (Radford et al. 2021, ICML) architecture, PLIP (Huang et al. 2023, Nat Med) as the pathology fine-tune, MI-Zero (Lu et al. 2023, CVPR) for slide-level zero-shot.
  • Segmentation — HoVer-Net — Joint Nuclei Seg + Classification for nuclei, CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification as the ViT successor, gland segmentation on GlaS — Gland Segmentation in Colon Histology (MICCAI 2015), multi-resolution methods.
  • Classification, biomarker prediction, survival — H&E-only mutation prediction, biomarker inference, survival modelling.
  • Mitosis detection — including the multi-domain MIDOG — MItosis DOmain Generalization Challenge benchmark.
  • Generative models — diffusion for synthesis, GAN-based stain normalisation.
  • Image registration — ANHIR, Learn2Reg challenges.
  • Clinical translation — workflow integration, computer-assisted triage, interpretability.

A useful single reference for a thesis introduction or a grant background section. The cutoff is ~mid-2023, so the very latest VLMs (CONCH, QuiltNet, MUSK), slide-level PFMs (GigaPath, Virchow, H-Optimus), and instruction-tuned pathology MLLMs (PathChat) are not covered.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The review is organised around the deep-learning pipeline for histopathology:

  1. Input — WSI formats, tissue masking, patch extraction, stain normalisation.
  2. Representation — patch encoders (ImageNet, pathology SSL, foundation models, vision-language).
  3. Aggregation — MIL aggregators from mean / max pooling through ABMIL / CLAM / TransMIL / graph MIL.
  4. Task heads — classification, segmentation, detection, regression for survival.
  5. Downstream applications — biomarker prediction, molecular alteration inference, prognosis stratification.
  6. Clinical integration — workflow, interpretability, regulatory considerations (lightly covered).

It does not attempt to be a meta-analysis or to rank methods quantitatively — it is an orientation review for newcomers and a reference index for experienced practitioners.

docs.title: Notable framings
docs.text:
• Author Liechty has a self-cited contribution on IDH mutation prediction from H&E in gliomas (Liechty et al. Sci Rep 2022) — the review uses this as a clinical-translation exemplar.
  • The Campanella 2019 clinical-grade demonstration is repeatedly cited as the scale precedent for weakly-supervised MIL.
  • Pathology foundation models are framed as the natural next step after CTransPath, with the review predating the UNI / GigaPath / Virchow wave (cutoff ~mid-2023 explains the relative thinness of the FM section relative to current-2026 standards).
  • Vision-language pathology is positioned as an emerging direction; PLIP and MI-Zero are highlighted as exemplars but the section is comparatively brief.

docs.title: Limitations (of the review itself)
docs.text:
• Coverage cutoff ~mid-2023 — does not cover CONCH, QuiltNet, MUSK, GigaPath, Virchow, H-Optimus, PathChat, PathGen, agentic pathology workflows.
  • Multimodal (path + omics + radiology) is treated relatively briefly — MCAT and Vanguri are cited but the broader multimodal stack is not surveyed in depth.
  • Clinical translation depth is uneven — deeper on deep-learning workflow than on regulatory / FDA / CE deployment considerations.
  • No leaderboard or per-task comparison tables — for quantitative comparison, link directly to the per-paper nodes.
  • Agentic pathology AI is out of scope (this branch is too recent for the cutoff).

docs.title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
docs.text: Maximilian Ilse, Jakub M. Tomczak, Max Welling · 2018 · ICML paper · doi · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before this paper, MIL pooling was dominated by fixed mean / max operators. ABMIL introduced learned scalar attention weights per instance, parameterised by a small two-layer MLP. The bag embedding becomes the attention-weighted sum of instance embeddings — permutation-invariant (preserving the MIL assumption) but trainable, and interpretable: attention weights yield free heatmap-style localisation of which patches drove the bag-level decision.

ABMIL seeded the modern WSI MIL literature in pathology. CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL, TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL, DSMIL, DTFD-MIL, SETMIL all descend from it.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
# pseudo-code: ABMIL attention head
H = encoder(instances)               # (N, D)
A = softmax(w.T @ tanh(V @ H.T))     # (1, N)
bag = (A @ H).squeeze()              # (D,)
y_hat = classifier(bag)

Two variants:

  • Vanilla attention — single non-linearity (tanh).
  • Gated attention — multiplies pre-softmax score by a separate sigmoid gate, often better-calibrated on harder bags.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: bag of instance embeddings (N × D), typically patch features from a CNN encoder.
  • Output: bag-level label + attention vector (N × 1) usable as a heatmap.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• MNIST bags — synthetic MIL benchmark.
  • Breast cancer histology — patch-level bags for slide-level positive/negative.
  • Colon cancer histology — same.
  • Camelyon16 — Cancer Metastases in Lymph Nodes 2016 is the standard pathology reuse benchmark for ABMIL today.
  • Metrics: AUC, accuracy.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Two-layer MLP attention head (configurable hidden dim).
  • Permutation-invariant pooling — the order of patches doesn't matter.
  • End-to-end trainable; backprop flows through both encoder and attention head.
  • No instance-instance interaction — each patch is scored in isolation (the key limitation addressed by TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL / DSMIL).

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: ABMIL outperforms mean- and max-pooling MIL, MI-Net, and MI-SVM on the synthetic MIL benchmarks and on the histology bags reported in the paper. The bigger contribution is the template — pathology MIL has used this attention head template ever since.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Permutation-invariant — ignores patch positions in the slide.
  • No instance-instance interaction — TransMIL/DSMIL add this later.
  • Single-class attention — multi-class extensions (CLAM-MB) need per-class branches.

docs.title: Clinical-grade computational pathology using weakly supervised deep learning on whole slide images
docs.text: Gabriele Campanella, Matthew G. Hanna, Luke Geneslaw et al. · 2019 · Nature Medicine doi · paper

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
This Nature Medicine 2019 paper demonstrated, at scale and in a clinical workflow, that weakly-supervised MIL on WSIs is feasible without per-patch annotation. The cohort is ~44,732 WSIs across three organ systems at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center:

  • Prostate core needle biopsies — 24,859 slides
  • Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) skin biopsies — 9,962 slides
  • Breast cancer metastasis to axillary lymph nodes — 9,894 slides

Labels are slide-level diagnostic reports alone — no pixel or patch annotation. The MIL pipeline (CNN feature extractor + RNN aggregator) achieves AUCs > 0.98 across all three tasks. The paper then defines a computer-assisted triage workflow in which the model labels slides as positive / negative; the pathologist reviews positives plus a sampled subset of negatives. Modelled to safely exclude 65–75% of confirmed-negative slides.

This is the clinical-grade scale precedent that motivated essentially every subsequent pathology MIL paper.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
• Slide-level labels mined from clinical diagnostic reports.
  • Per-slide MIL training: CNN encoder + RNN aggregator with top-k instance selection.
  • Massive distributed training on internal MSKCC compute.
  • Calibrate the operating point for a clinical triage target (high sensitivity, acceptable specificity for negative exclusion).

docs.title: Clinical framing
docs.text: Aspect Detail Clinical problem Diagnostic triage of routine surgical pathology — prostate / BCC / breast axillary Cohort design Retrospective MSKCC cohort, slide-level labels from clinical reports Clinical workflow AI triage: pathologist reviews AI-positive + sampled negatives Clinical endpoint Cancer-presence detection AUC; safe-exclusion fraction at high sensitivity Clinical need for AI Workload bottleneck + inter-observer variability for early-stage cancer detection

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Internal MSKCC cohorts (cannot be released).
  • Tasks: slide-level tumor detection in prostate biopsies, BCC skin biopsies, breast axillary nodes.
  • Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, safe-exclusion fraction at fixed sensitivity.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• ResNet-style CNN feature extractor.
  • RNN-based MIL aggregator with top-k instance selection.
  • Bag-instance mining to handle gigapixel bag size.
  • Slide-level cross-entropy + clinical triage calibration.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: AUC > 0.98 across all three tasks. The triage workflow could safely exclude 65–75% of confirmed-negative slides at full sensitivity, freeing pathologist time substantially.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Internal MSKCC data — external replication is impossible from scratch.
  • RNN aggregator is superseded by attention / Transformer MIL (ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning / CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL / TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL).
  • Retrospective — clinical-grade claim ultimately requires prospective deployment study.

docs.title: CellViT: Vision Transformers for precise cell segmentation and classification
docs.text: Fabian Hörst, Moritz Rempe, Lukas Heine et al. · 2024 · Medical Image Analysis doi · paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: HoVer-Net (Graham et al. 2019, Med Image Anal) solved the touching-nuclei instance-separation problem in 2019 with its HV-decoder trick. By 2023 the CNN encoder was the weakest link: a SAM- or DINOv2-pretrained ViT delivers richer, less stain-sensitive features with minimal architectural change. CellViT realises this swap: keep HoVer-Net's three-decoder head, replace the encoder with a SAM-pretrained ViT, and gain substantial PanNuke improvements at the cost of model size.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
H&E patch → SAM-pretrained ViT-B (or ViT-H) encoder
   ↓
   → NP decoder      (nuclear pixel mask)
   → HV decoder      (horizontal-vertical distance maps)
   → NT decoder      (nuclear type)
post-processing: same watershed-style instance separation as HoVer-Net

Two released variants:

  • CellViT-256 — SAM-pretrained ViT-B, 256×256 input.
  • CellViT-SAM-H — SAM-pretrained ViT-H, 1024×1024 input (more accurate, slower).

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch (256×256 or 1024×1024 depending on variant).
  • Output: per-pixel instance ID + per-nucleus class label.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Primary benchmark: PanNuke — Pan-Cancer Nuclei Seg & Classification.
  • Metrics: PQ, Dice, F1.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Encoder: SAM-pretrained ViT (B or H).
  • Three decoder branches adapted from HoVer-Net's NP / HV / NT structure.
  • Joint multi-task training; cross-entropy + Dice + MSE losses.

docs.title: Main results

docs.title: Data-efficient and weakly supervised computational pathology on whole-slide images
docs.text: Ming Y. Lu, Drew F. K. Williamson, Tiffany Y. Chen et al. · 2021 · Nature Biomedical Engineering doi · paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
CLAM is the most-cited and most-deployed weakly-supervised MIL framework in pathology in 2021–2025. Two reasons:

  1. It produces reliable accuracy on slide-level classification across many cancer subtype and detection tasks while being simpler and faster than later Transformer-based aggregators.
  2. The open-source pipeline at mahmoodlab/CLAM covers the entire WSI workflow: tissue segmentation, patch extraction, feature extraction (any backbone), MIL training, and attention-heatmap generation. It is the toolkit that other PFM evaluations are built on.

Modern PFM benchmarks (UNI, GigaPath, Virchow) commonly run "PFM features → CLAM head" as their default MIL evaluation.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
CLAM extends ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning along two axes:

  1. Per-class attention branches (CLAM-MB): one attention map per class instead of one shared map. CLAM-SB keeps a single attention map and a slide-level softmax — usually adequate for binary tasks.
  2. Instance-level clustering loss: highest-attended patches per class are positive pseudo-labels for an auxiliary classifier; lowest-attended are negative. This regularises attention and improves data efficiency when slide counts are small (a few hundred per class).

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: bag of patch features per WSI (from any encoder — ResNet-50 / CTransPath / UNI / GigaPath).
  • Output: slide-level class probabilities + per-class attention heatmaps (interpretable lesion localisation as a free byproduct).

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Renal cell carcinoma subtyping (TCGA-RCC).
  • Non-small cell lung cancer subtyping (TCGA-NSCLC).
  • Breast cancer metastasis detection (Camelyon16 — Cancer Metastases in Lymph Nodes 2016).
  • Metrics: AUC, accuracy, F1.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Patch features from ResNet-50 ImageNet (original) or any modern PFM (current practice).
  • Per-class attention MLPs → per-class bag embeddings → per-class scores.
  • Instance-clustering loss with attention-derived pseudo-labels.
  • Adam, dropout, standard end-to-end training.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: CLAM outperforms ABMIL, MIL-RNN, and mean / max pooling on all three tasks. Data-efficiency ablations show ~70% AUC with as few as 100 training slides — a meaningful threshold for rare-subtype studies.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Permutation-invariant — no spatial modelling beyond patch features (see TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL for a sequence-aware alternative).
  • Pseudo-labels can be noisy in tumour-rich slides where both top- and bottom-attended patches contain tumour.
  • Original backbone is dated — modern accuracy gain comes mostly from upgrading the patch encoder (UNI / GigaPath / Virchow).

docs.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
docs.text: Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy et al. · 2021 · ICML paper · github · doi

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
CLIP is not a pathology paper, but it is the architectural foundation of every modern pathology vision-language model. PLIP, CONCH, QuiltNet, MUSK, and MI-Zero are all CLIP-architecture or CLIP-initialised models fine-tuned on pathology data. Any pathology VL discussion that doesn't reference CLIP is incomplete.

The contribution is scale + simplicity: a dual-encoder (image + text), an InfoNCE contrastive objective, 400M (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web. The result is a model that does zero-shot image classification by encoding candidate class names as text and picking the closest text to the image — without seeing a single labelled image.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
image batch → image encoder → I (B, D)
text batch  → text encoder  → T (B, D)
similarity matrix S = I · T.T  → diagonal positives, off-diagonal negatives
loss = cross-entropy on rows (img→txt) + cross-entropy on cols (txt→img)

At inference, zero-shot classification:

prompt_k = template.format(class_name_k)
text_emb_k = text_encoder(prompt_k)
prob(class_k | image) ∝ exp(<image_emb, text_emb_k>)

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: RGB image + text prompt.
  • Output: image embedding, text embedding, zero-shot class probabilities.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Pretraining: WIT (WebImageText) — 400M (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web (OpenAI-internal, not released).
  • Evaluation: 27+ benchmarks including ImageNet, CIFAR, Birdsnap, Food101, etc.
  • Metrics: top-1 / top-5 accuracy in zero-shot, linear-probe, and full fine-tuning settings.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Image encoders: ResNet-50/101/RN50x4/RN50x16/RN50x64 + ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14.
  • Text encoder: 12-layer Transformer (similar to GPT-2 small).
  • Loss: symmetric cross-entropy on the similarity matrix.
  • Training: large batch (~32k), mixed-precision, ~14 days on hundreds of GPUs.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: CLIP zero-shot matches or exceeds supervised ResNet-50 on ImageNet without seeing any ImageNet training images. Across 27 datasets, zero-shot CLIP is competitive with fully-supervised baselines. The release of code + weights (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14, RN50, RN101, etc.) sparked the entire VLM era.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Pretraining data not released — reproduction needs LAION or similar.
  • Natural-image + web-text domain — direct application to pathology fails without fine-tuning (PLIP (Huang et al. 2023, Nat Med), CONCH).
  • Prompt-engineering sensitivity — small prompt changes shift accuracy.
  • No clinical text training — medical / pathology terminology is out-of-distribution.

docs.title: Transformer-based unsupervised contrastive learning for histopathological image classification
docs.text: Xiyue Wang, Sen Yang, Jun Zhang et al. · 2022 · Medical Image Analysis doi · paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
CTransPath was, for ~18 months in 2022–2023, the strongest open-source pathology SSL checkpoint and the canonical patch encoder for many WSI MIL pipelines. It was the first widely-used demonstration that a Transformer backbone, pretrained on TCGA-scale pathology data with a carefully designed contrastive objective, beats both ImageNet-pretrained CNNs and earlier pathology SSL recipes (SimCLR-pathology, MoCo-v3-ImageNet).

CTransPath was superseded by larger foundation models (UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2), GigaPath, Virchow) by 2024, but it remains the standard open-weights compute-cheap baseline and the pre-UNI reference in PFM comparison tables.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
• Backbone: Swin Transformer Tiny (~28M params), modified for SSL.
  • Objective: SRCL — Semantically-Relevant Contrastive Learning. A MoCo v3 variant that augments the standard contrastive pair with semantically-related positives drawn from a learned memory bank, encouraging the encoder to group visually similar patches across slides.
  • Pretraining data: ~32k WSIs (TCGA + PAIP), ~15M H&E patches at 224×224.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch, 224×224.
  • Output: 768-dim patch embedding.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Downstream evaluation in the paper covers patch classification, MIL slide-level classification, and retrieval across multiple pathology benchmarks.
  • Metrics: AUC, accuracy, top-k accuracy.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Swin-T encoder + projection head.
  • MoCo v3-style momentum encoder + memory bank.
  • SRCL augmentation: semantic positives drawn from the memory bank using feature similarity.
  • Standard contrastive InfoNCE loss + SRCL positive term.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: CTransPath outperforms ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 / ViT, SimCLR-pathology, and MoCo v3 on multiple downstream pathology tasks. The release of code + weights enabled wide adoption: CTransPath became the de-facto open patch encoder for pathology MIL pipelines in 2022–2023.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Smaller backbone (~28M) than modern PFMs (UNI ViT-L ~307M, Virchow ViT-H ~632M).
  • Limited pretraining cohort (TCGA + PAIP) — less stain diversity than 100k+ WSI PFMs.
  • Embedding dim 768 vs UNI's 1024 — small representation cost downstream.
  • No vision-language alignment — pure patch SSL.

docs.title: Hover-Net: Simultaneous segmentation and classification of nuclei in multi-tissue histology images
docs.text: Simon Graham, Quoc Dang Vu, Shan E. Ahmed Raza et al. · 2019 · Medical Image Analysis doi · paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Touching nuclei break naive connected-components instance segmentation. HoVer-Net introduces a single-stage CNN with three decoders that solves nuclei instance segmentation + classification in one forward pass, using a horizontal-vertical (HV) distance-map decoder to drive watershed-style separation of touching nuclei.

The HV-decoder template has been reused by CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification and many other follow-ups; HoVer-Net remains the canonical CNN baseline for cell-level H&E analysis.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Three decoder branches share a Pre-Act ResNet encoder:

  1. NP decoder — nuclear pixel mask (binary foreground vs background).
  2. HV decoder — per-pixel signed distance from the nucleus centre in x and y.
  3. NT decoder — per-nucleus class label (when annotations are available).

Post-processing:

seeds = local minima of |∇HV|
mask  = NP > threshold
instances = watershed(mask, seeds)
class[i] = mode(NT[instances == i])

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch, typically 256×256 at 40×.
  • Output: per-pixel instance ID + per-nucleus class label.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• CoNSeP (introduced in this paper), Kumar, CPM, PanNuke — Pan-Cancer Nuclei Seg & Classification.
  • Tasks: nuclei instance segmentation, nuclei classification (4–6 classes depending on dataset).
  • Metrics: PQ, Dice, AJI, F1.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Encoder: Pre-Act ResNet-50.
  • Three decoder branches with task-specific upsampling.
  • Loss: combination of cross-entropy (NP, NT) + MSE (HV) + Dice (NP) with carefully tuned weights.
  • Watershed post-processing on the HV gradient.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: HoVer-Net outperforms Mask R-CNN, Micro-Net, and DCAN on CoNSeP / Kumar / CPM at release. Remains a strong PanNuke baseline today (modern ViT-based methods like CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification surpass it but cite it as the reference).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Multi-task loss balancing is sensitive — paper provides ratios, ad-hoc cohorts need re-tuning.
  • Watershed post-processing is the inference bottleneck at WSI scale.
  • CNN backbone is dated; CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification addresses this.
  • H&E only — IHC / multiplex IF need re-training.

docs.title: Visual Language Pretrained Multiple Instance Zero-Shot Transfer for Histopathology Images
docs.text: Ming Y. Lu, Bowen Chen, Andrew Zhang et al. · 2023 · CVPR doi · paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
PLIP (Huang et al. 2023, Nat Med) and other patch-level pathology VLMs perform zero-shot classification on patches, but most clinically meaningful pathology tasks are slide-level. MI-Zero is the first widely-cited method that bridges patch-VL → slide-level zero-shot, without any slide-level training. The key insight: aggregate patch-level VL similarity scores against a text prompt over the slide's patches using simple pooling — top-k, weighted top-k, or identity — producing a slide-level zero-shot prediction.

MI-Zero enabled the modern slide-level zero-shot WSI pipeline and is the seed paper for CONCH-MIL and other slide-level VL methods.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
for each patch p in slide S:
    score(p, class_k) = <image_enc(p), text_enc(prompt_k)>
slide_score(class_k) = top_k_pool({score(p, class_k) for p in S})
prediction(S) = argmax_k slide_score(class_k)

Three pooling functions explored: top-k mean, weighted top-k, identity (mean over all patches). Top-k mean is the default — it captures the strongest patch-level VL evidence per class while ignoring the long tail of weak signals.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: WSI patch bag + text prompts (one per class).
  • Output: slide-level zero-shot class probability (no slide-level training).

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• TCGA-NSCLC subtyping.
  • TCGA-RCC subtyping.
  • TCGA-BRCA subtyping.
  • Metrics: zero-shot accuracy, AUC, balanced accuracy.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Patch-level VL encoder: any pathology VLM (the authors use a contemporaneous Mahmood-Lab model; PLIP can be substituted).
  • Patch-level similarity score against each candidate text prompt.
  • Aggregation across the slide's patches via top-k pooling.
  • No training at slide level.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: MI-Zero achieves competitive zero-shot performance on TCGA-NSCLC, TCGA-RCC, TCGA-BRCA — closing the gap to fully-supervised MIL on the easier tasks. The aggregation choice (top-k pooling, k ≈ 25 in the paper) matters more than alternative complicated schemes.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Zero-shot lags supervised on most tasks — useful for label-poor regimes.
  • Prompt-sensitive — small prompt changes shift accuracy noticeably.
  • Patch encoder quality dominates — the choice of pathology VLM upstream matters more than the aggregation details.
  • Top-k aggregation is coarse — under-weights diffuse signal across many low-attention patches; misses subtle patterns.

docs.text: Zhi Huang, Federico Bianchi, Mert Yuksekgonul et al. · 2023 · Nature Medicine doi · paper · github · huggingface

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before PLIP, pathology vision-language work was scattered: small captioning datasets (ARCH), CLIP-pretrained-on-natural-images applied off-the-shelf, ad-hoc image-text models on limited corpora. PLIP is the first widely-cited, open-weights pathology vision-language foundation model, and it ships with the OpenPath dataset — ~200k pathology image-caption pairs mined from medical Twitter (clinician posts using pathology-related hashtags) — the first large-scale public pathology image-caption corpus.

PLIP enabled the first zero-shot pathology image classification pipelines and is now the standard open-weights reference in the pathology VL space.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
• Take CLIP (Radford et al. 2021, ICML) ViT-B/32.
  • Mine ~200k pathology image-caption pairs from medical Twitter — the OpenPath corpus.
  • Fine-tune CLIP with standard InfoNCE on OpenPath.
  • Release weights + dataset.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch + pathology text prompt.
  • Output: image embedding, text embedding, zero-shot class probabilities.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Pretraining: OpenPath (~200k pathology image-caption pairs from medical Twitter).
  • Downstream evaluation: Kather CRC, PanNuke — Pan-Cancer Nuclei Seg & Classification patch crops, others.
  • Metrics: zero-shot accuracy, top-k retrieval, precision-at-k.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Architecture: CLIP ViT-B/32 + text Transformer.
  • Training: InfoNCE on (image, caption) pairs.
  • Inference: text prompts → zero-shot class probability via dot product on shared embedding space.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: PLIP outperforms CLIP-ImageNet on multiple pathology zero-shot benchmarks and matches or exceeds several supervised baselines (without per-task labels). Image-text retrieval works well across pathology corpora.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Twitter captions are noisy — clinical fidelity varies.
  • ViT-B/32 backbone is small by modern PFM standards — newer pathology VLMs (CONCH, QuiltNet) use larger encoders and more curated corpora.
  • Common-finding bias — Twitter posts skew to common findings; rare conditions are under-represented.
  • Patch-level only — slide-level zero-shot needs MI-Zero (Lu et al. 2023, CVPR) or CONCH-MIL.
  • Ethical / consent concerns — Twitter-mined data; subsequent VLMs (CONCH, QuiltNet) use textbook sources to avoid this issue.

docs.title: TransMIL: Transformer based Correlated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole Slide Image Classification
docs.text: Zhuchen Shao, Hao Bian, Yang Chen et al. · 2021 · NeurIPS paper · github

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning and CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL score each patch in isolation — the MIL assumption is permutation-invariant pooling. But tumour tissue is spatially organised: lesions are contiguous, immune infiltration is contextual, gland architecture only makes sense across multiple patches. TransMIL is the first widely adopted MIL variant that explicitly models instance-instance correlations at gigapixel scale via Transformer self-attention.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
patches → linear proj → [CLS] + sequence
   → PPEG (multi-scale spatial conv)
   → Nyström-attention Transformer layers
   → [CLS] embedding → classifier

Two key ingredients:

  1. Nyström self-attention — drops attention cost from O(N²) to O(N), making bags of thousands of patches tractable.
  2. PPEG (Pyramid Position Encoding Generator) — re-injects 2-D spatial context via multi-scale convolutions on the bag, restoring spatial signal lost in the otherwise permutation-invariant Transformer sequence.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: bag of patch features per WSI (from any encoder).
  • Output: slide-level class probability.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Camelyon16 — Cancer Metastases in Lymph Nodes 2016 — breast lymph-node metastasis (binary).
  • TCGA-NSCLC — non-small cell lung cancer subtyping.
  • TCGA-RCC — renal cell carcinoma subtyping.
  • Metrics: AUC, accuracy, F1.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Default ResNet-50 ImageNet features (paper); modern practice swaps for UNI / GigaPath features.
  • 2-layer Nyström Transformer encoder.
  • PPEG between Transformer layers.
  • [CLS] token pooling for slide-level prediction.
  • Standard cross-entropy training; Adam optimiser.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: TransMIL outperforms ABMIL, CLAM, DSMIL, and MIL-RNN on all three benchmarks. Ablations show PPEG positional encoding provides meaningful improvement over random 2-D mixing, validating the need for explicit spatial signal.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Approximate attention — Nyström introduces variance; exact attention on small bags can outperform.
  • Parameter cost — adds Transformer parameters vs ABMIL/CLAM.
  • Less interpretable than CLAM's per-class attention branches — visualising "what the Transformer attends to" requires extra work.
  • Default backbone (ResNet-50) is dated.

docs.title: How Claude should use this article
docs.text:
skill · articles

Reach for TransMIL when instance-instance correlations are likely informative: survival prediction, complex subtyping, spatial architectural cues. Cite alongside CLAM (Lu et al. 2021, Nat Biomed Eng) and ABMIL (Ilse, Tomczak, Welling 2018) as the standard MIL benchmark triple.

docs.title: Towards a General-Purpose Foundation Model for Computational Pathology
docs.text: Richard J. Chen, Tong Ding, Ming Y. Lu et al. · 2024 · Nature Medicine doi · github · huggingface

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Before UNI, pathology pipelines mostly relied on ImageNet-pretrained CNNs or a handful of pathology-specific encoders (CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit-DINO). UNI is one of the first pathology foundation models that explicitly targets general-purpose patch-level representations across many tissue types, evaluated on a broad downstream suite (33 tasks at slide and patch level). Together with GigaPath, Virchow, H-Optimus, and CONCH, it anchors the modern PFM cohort that any new method should benchmark against.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text: Train a ViT-L/16 with the DINOv2 self-supervised recipe on Mass-100K, an internal corpus of ~100k H&E whole-slide images (~100M patches) spanning ~20 tissue types. Use the resulting frozen encoder as a drop-in feature extractor for downstream classification, MIL aggregation (ABMIL/CLAM/TransMIL), and retrieval.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patches (commonly 256×256 or 224×224 at ~20× / 0.5 μm/px).
  • Output: per-patch embedding (ViT-L hidden dim — typically 1024).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Architecture: ViT-L/16 (~307M parameters).
  • Objective: DINOv2 (self-distillation with masked image modelling).
  • Pretraining data: Mass-100K (~100k WSIs, ~100M patches, internal — not publicly redistributable).
  • Compute: large-scale GPU pretraining (paper reports detailed setup).
  • Downstream evaluation: 33 tasks across patch-level classification, slide-level MIL, and retrieval, compared against ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 / ViT, CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit-DINO.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• Pretraining: Mass-100K (internal).
  • Eval datasets (selected): 33-task evaluation benchmark covering many public datasets — see paper for the full list.
  • Tasks: tissue-type classification, tumor-vs-normal, subtype classification, grading, biomarker prediction, slide-level survival proxies.
  • Metrics: AUC, balanced accuracy, top-k accuracy.

docs.title: Main results
docs.text: UNI generally outperforms ImageNet baselines and prior pathology PFMs (CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit-DINO) on the majority of downstream tasks under frozen-feature evaluation, with consistent gains on rare-tissue and few-shot settings. See the paper for per-task numbers — this page does not reproduce metrics to avoid drift.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Pretraining data not redistributable — Mass-100K is internal, blocking from-scratch reproduction.
  • Patch-level only in the primary release — slide-level objectives require downstream MIL or pooling (consider GigaPath for slide-level pretraining).
  • H&E only — IHC/IF tasks need a different encoder.
  • Gated weights on Hugging Face — pipelines requiring fully open weights should consider CTransPath or open ViT alternatives.

UNI is a canonical baseline in any new WSI-level benchmark. When the user asks to compare PFMs, cite UNI alongside CTransPath, GigaPath, Virchow, H-Optimus, and CONCH. When UNI2 is added, link via supersedes and update method-comparison tables.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
BACH is the ICIAR 2018 challenge dataset for four-class breast histology classification on H&E. Two parts:

  • Part A: 400 microscopy images (2040×1536, ~0.42 μm/px), 100 per class — normal, benign, in-situ carcinoma, invasive carcinoma.
  • Part B: 10 H&E WSIs (.svs) with pixel-level 4-class annotations for WSI-level inference evaluation.

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organ: breast
  • Disease: breast cancer (full spectrum: normal → invasive)
  • Species: human
  • Specimen type: microscopy images (Part A) and whole-slide images (Part B)

docs.title: Tasks and metrics
docs.text: Part Task Metric A 4-class image classification Accuracy (primary), precision, recall B Pixel-level 4-class WSI labelling Per-class Dice / accuracy

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Hosted at iciar2018-challenge.grand-challenge.org. Requires registration. Released under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 — non-commercial, no derivatives, attribution required.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
Part A images come at native 2040×1536 pixels. Common pipeline:

  1. Load TIFs at native resolution.
  2. Stain normalisation (Macenko / Reinhard / Vahadane) — staining varies significantly between batches; reported BACH numbers swing with the normalisation choice.
  3. Random 512×512 crops at training time + standard rotation / flip augmentation.
  4. Part B WSIs: read .svs via OpenSlide (WSI I/O), sliding-window inference at the patch resolution chosen for Part A.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: BACH gives a clean 4-class breast classification task with morphology-only labels (no molecular subtypes), making it a popular stress-test for stain robustness and few-shot transfer from pathology PFMs. The dataset is small enough to be used as a transfer-learning benchmark even on a single GPU.

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Only 100 images per class — heavy augmentation / SSL pretraining is mandatory; from-scratch CNNs overfit immediately.
  • Stain variance dominates reported variance between methods. Always declare which stain normaliser (if any) was used.
  • Class boundaries (benign vs in-situ vs invasive) follow specific consensus criteria — labels are not directly portable to other breast cohorts.
  • Part B has only 10 WSIs — use it for qualitative localisation maps, not slide-level metrics.

docs.title: How Claude should use this dataset
docs.text:
skill · datasets

Treat BACH as the small-data complement to Camelyon16 — Camelyon16 stresses scale, BACH stresses stain robustness and few-shot transfer. Frequently cited together when validating pathology foundation models on breast tissue.

docs.text: h-and-e · lymph-node, breast · 400 slides · CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication) per grand-challenge release; verify on the data page before redistribution homepage · download · doi · license · access

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
Camelyon16 is the founding public benchmark for breast cancer metastasis detection in sentinel lymph nodes on H&E WSIs. The release contains 400 whole-slide images (270 training + 130 test) contributed by Radboud University Medical Center and Utrecht University Medical Center.

Each slide is labelled at three granularities:

  • Slide-level: negative / isolated tumor cells (ITC) / micrometastasis / macrometastasis.
  • Lesion-level: exhaustive polygons around contiguous tumor regions on positive slides (XML/JSON).
  • Pixel-level: derived tumor masks from the lesion polygons.

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organ: lymph node (sentinel) — breast-cancer specimen
  • Disease: breast cancer with regional metastasis
  • Species: human
  • Specimen type: sentinel lymph node sections

docs.title: Tasks and metrics
docs.text:
Task Metric Slide-level tumor presence AUC Lesion-level detection FROC (free-response ROC) — the headline challenge metric Pixel segmentation Dice (secondary)

FROC measures sensitivity at fixed false-positive-per-image counts and is the standard against which weakly supervised MIL pipelines are reported.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
Hosted via the grand-challenge platform (camelyon17.grand-challenge.org/Data/ is the canonical data page for both editions). Registration required. Released under CC0 — the data are public-domain dedicated, but redistribution should still cite the JAMA 2017 challenge paper.

The full release is ~750 GB (to verify); budget time for Aspera / S3 download.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
import openslide
slide = openslide.OpenSlide("/data/camelyon16/training/tumor/tumor_001.tif")
print(slide.level_dimensions, slide.properties.get("openslide.mpp-x"))

Standard pipeline:

  1. Read .tif via OpenSlide (WSI I/O) — handles Aperio / Hamamatsu vendor blocks.
  2. Tissue mask at level 4-6 (downsample) → keep only foreground patches.
  3. Patch at 20× or 40× (challenge slides have 40× level); 256×256 conventional for MIL.
  4. Build positive/negative patch labels from the XML tumor polygons.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Camelyon16 is the seed dataset for the entire weakly-supervised MIL literature in pathology — ABMIL, CLAM, TransMIL, DSMIL, DTFD-MIL all report Camelyon16 numbers. Any new WSI classification method without a Camelyon16 number is treated with suspicion.

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Two-centre, two-scanner drift — Pannoramic 250 Flash (Radboud) vs Aperio (Utrecht). Stain and resolution differ.
  • Lesion vs slide metrics tell different stories — high AUC with low FROC means the model is voting correctly but localising poorly.
  • ITC may be under-annotated — exhaustive polygons cover the main contiguous lesion only.
  • Camelyon17 is a different challenge (patient-level pN staging on 1000 slides from 5 centres) — do not conflate.

docs.text:

Camelyon16 is the first benchmark to run when proposing a new WSI classification / MIL method. Always pair slide-AUC with lesion-FROC.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
GlaS is the canonical small benchmark for colon gland instance segmentation on H&E. The release contains:

  • 165 ROI images (cropped from 16 source WSIs) at ~0.62 μm/px.
  • One instance mask per gland, encoded as colour-coded BMPs (one colour per instance).
  • Histology grade per image: benign or malignant.
  • Splits: 85 training, 80 test — split further into Test A (60, easier) and Test B (20, harder).

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organ: colon
  • Disease: colorectal cancer (benign and malignant)
  • Species: human
  • Specimen type: ROI crops from WSIs

docs.title: Tasks and metrics
docs.text:
Task Metric Gland instance segmentation F1 detection, Object-Dice, Object-Hausdorff Benign vs malignant classification Per-class accuracy

The three official metrics each test a different property: F1 measures detection, Object-Dice measures pixel agreement per-instance, Object-Hausdorff measures boundary fidelity (shape).

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Distributed via the Tissue Image Analytics Centre at Warwick: warwick.ac.uk/fac/cross_fac/tia/data/glascontest/. No registration needed for the data itself; research-use citation expected.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np
img = np.array(Image.open("train_1.bmp"))
mask = np.array(Image.open("train_1_anno.bmp"))   # colour-coded instances

Common pipeline:

  1. Load BMP/TIF images at native resolution.
  2. Preserve colour mode when reading masks — converting to grayscale collapses instances.
  3. Convert colour-coded masks to integer label maps (one int per instance).
  4. Random crop / flip / rotate; gland shapes are scale-variant — colour-jitter alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Despite its small size, GlaS remains the first stop for any new gland or instance segmentation method in pathology. The Test A / Test B split forces methods to report performance under increased difficulty, exposing brittle models.

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Very small (165 images) — heavy augmentation mandatory; without it, deep models overfit immediately.
  • Two test splits — always report Test A and Test B separately. Aggregated numbers hide the Test B drop.
  • Metric implementations differ between reimplementations. The original Matlab reference and the more recent community Python ports are not bit-identical; cite the implementation used.
  • Colour-coded BMP masks are easy to corrupt — loading in L (grayscale) mode collapses all instances into one.
  • Single-centre source — generalisation to other colon cohorts is unproven.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
MIDOG is the canonical multi-domain mitosis-detection benchmark on H&E. The release combines high-power-field (HPF) annotations across multiple scanners, institutions, and tumour types:

  • Human breast cancer
  • Canine cutaneous mast cell tumour (the original 2021 cohort)
  • Melanoma (human and canine)
  • Neuroendocrine tumour
  • Lymphoma

Annotations are mitotic-figure centre points + class label (true mitosis vs hard-negative "lookalike"). Editions: MIDOG 2021, 2022, 2025 — each adds new tumour cohorts; cite the edition explicitly.

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organs: breast, skin, lung, lymph node, soft tissue (varies by edition)
  • Disease: cancers with mitotic-count-driven grading
  • Species: human + canine (cross-species design is intentional)
  • Specimen type: WSIs cropped to annotated HPFs

docs.title: Tasks and metrics
docs.text: Task Metric Mitotic figure detection F1 at fixed IoU / centre-distance tolerance (primary), precision, recall Mitosis vs lookalike classification AP

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Distributed at imig.science/midog. Requires registration. CC BY 4.0 for training data; test data held by the organisers for ongoing evaluation submissions.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
import openslide, json
slide = openslide.OpenSlide("/data/midog/001.tif")
ann = json.load(open("/data/midog/midog2022_annotations.json"))

Pipeline:

  1. Read .tif via OpenSlide (WSI I/O).
  2. Only score detections inside the provided HPF regions — annotations are exhaustive only there. Outside HPFs the "ground truth" is undefined; counting false positives outside inflates error unfairly.
  3. Patch at 40× (~0.25 μm/px) — mitotic figures are only ~10–20 pixels wide.
  4. Mine hard-negative lookalikes from the released annotations — they are the major source of false positives.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: MIDOG is explicitly built to break single-domain models: training on one scanner + tumour type and testing on others produces sharp degradation, which is the point. It is the standard benchmark for domain generalisation in pathology and for prognostic mitotic-count workflows (mitoses per area is a routine grading input in clinical pathology).

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Annotations are HPF-region-bounded — running detection outside those regions inflates false positives.
  • Cross-scanner / cross-tumour drift is the point — naive single-domain training collapses; reviewers expect explicit domain-generalisation or domain-adaptation reporting.
  • Mitotic figures are tiny (~10–20 px at 40×) — ImageNet-style downsizing destroys them.
  • Ordinal mitotic counts (per ROI) feed prognostic grading systems — calibrate count thresholds against pathologist consensus before clinical claims.
  • Edition matters — 2021 was canine-only-ish, 2022 added cohorts, 2025 again — always cite the edition.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
PANDA is the largest public dataset for prostate Gleason / ISUP grading on H&E biopsies. It bundles ~10,616 WSIs (to verify) contributed by two institutions:

  • Radboud University Medical Center (Radboudumc), the Netherlands
  • Karolinska Institute, Sweden

Each slide is a prostate needle-biopsy core scanned at high resolution (multi-resolution TIFF readable with OpenSlide / pyvips). Labels include ISUP grade group (0–5), Gleason primary/secondary patterns, and partial pixel-level tumour annotations on a subset.

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organ: prostate
  • Disease: prostate adenocarcinoma
  • Species: human
  • Specimen type: needle biopsy (not radical prostatectomy)

docs.title: Labels and tasks
docs.text:
• isup-grade — ordinal 0–5
  • gleason-primary, gleason-secondary — Gleason pattern pair
  • tumor-mask — partial pixel-level annotations (subset)

Standard tasks:

  • Grading — ISUP grade group classification (the original challenge).
  • Subtype classification — Gleason pattern.
  • Tumor region segmentation — on the annotated subset.

Original challenge metric: quadratic-weighted kappa.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:

License terms come from the Kaggle competition rules; verify the current text via the rules page before any redistribution.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
import openslide
slide = openslide.OpenSlide("/path/to/0005f7aaab2800f6170c399693a96917.tiff")
print(slide.level_dimensions, slide.properties.get("openslide.mpp-x"))

Recommended flow:

  1. Read TIFF WSIs with OpenSlide or pyvips.
  2. Tissue masking to drop background.
  3. Patch at 20× (or 10× for compute-bound runs); 256×256 patches are common.
  4. Harmonise across the two centres — Radboud and Karolinska annotated under different protocols. Always evaluate per-source as well as combined.

docs.title: Used by benchmarks
docs.text: • WSI-PFM benchmark (node not yet ingested — pending §11.6 user decision)

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Two source institutions with different annotation protocols → cross-source generalisation is non-trivial; report per-centre metrics.
  • Karolinska subset has known label noise; community-cleaned variants exist.
  • Heavy class imbalance toward ISUP grade 0 (benign).

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
PanNuke is the standard public benchmark for nuclei instance segmentation and 5-class classification on H&E. The release contains:

  • ~7,901 patches at 256×256 pixels.
  • 19 tissue types (breast, colon, lung, prostate, stomach, kidney, ovary, bladder, pancreas, skin, thyroid, liver, cervix, bile duct, oesophagus, testis, uterus, head & neck, adrenal gland).
  • Instance masks + per-instance 5-class labels: neoplastic, inflammatory, connective, dead, epithelial.
  • Official 3-fold split — use it for cross-method comparability.

docs.title: Modalities and scope
docs.text:
• Modality: H&E
  • Organs: 19 tissues spanning common cancer sites
  • Disease: pan-cancer
  • Species: human
  • Specimen type: 256×256 patches (pre-cropped — no WSI context)

docs.title: Tasks and metrics
docs.text:
Task Metric Nuclei instance segmentation PQ (Panoptic Quality), DQ (detection), SQ (segmentation) 5-class nuclei classification Multi-class PQ per class

PQ is the canonical metric. Per-class PQ is reported alongside binary PQ because class 4 (Dead) is rare and easily inflates / deflates the mean.

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Hosted at jgamper.github.io/PanNukeDataset. No registration. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — non-commercial, share-alike.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
import numpy as np
images = np.load("Fold_1/images/fold1/images.npy")    # (N, 256, 256, 3)
masks  = np.load("Fold_1/masks/fold1/masks.npy")      # (N, 256, 256, 6) one-hot per class + bg

Pipeline:

  1. Load .npy arrays (images + masks) — no WSI reader needed; patches are already cut.
  2. Convert per-class one-hot stacks → per-class integer instance maps.
  3. Use the official 3-fold split shipped with the release. Ad-hoc splits invalidate comparisons.
  4. Strong colour augmentation across folds — stain varies across the 19 tissues.
  5. Evaluate using the official PanNuke-metrics repo — PQ has tissue-edge cases that ad-hoc implementations get wrong.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: PanNuke is the first benchmark to run for any nuclei-level model in pathology — HoVer-Net, CellViT, StarDist, and follow-ups all report PanNuke PQ. Coverage across 19 tissues makes it a meaningful test for generalisation beyond a single organ.

docs.title: Known pitfalls
docs.text:
• Patches are pre-cropped — no tissue context beyond 256×256; methods relying on broader context cannot use it directly.
  • Class 4 (Dead) is rare; mean PQ can hide poor performance on it. Always report per-class PQ.
  • Stain variance across 19 tissues is large — naive training without colour augmentation underperforms.
  • Use the official 3-fold split. Self-defined splits break cross-paper comparison.
  • Use the official PQ implementation (PanNuke-metrics repo) — community reimplementations diverge on edge cases (empty patches, boundary tiles).

docs.title: Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning (ABMIL)
docs.text:
stage: deep_wsi_learning · parents: weakly-supervised-mil

Replace permutation-invariant pooling (mean / max) over instances with a learned attention mechanism. Each instance produces a scalar attention weight via a small two-layer MLP; the bag embedding is the attention-weighted sum of instance embeddings. The attention weights are interpretable — they highlight which patches drove the slide-level prediction, providing free heatmap-style localisation.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before ABMIL, MIL pooling was dominated by mean and max — both fixed and uninformative. ABMIL introduced a learned scalar attention weight per instance, parameterised by a small two-layer MLP. The bag embedding becomes the attention-weighted sum of instance embeddings:

α_k = softmax(w^T tanh(V h_k))
bag_emb = Σ_k α_k * h_k

This is permutation-invariant (still satisfies the MIL assumption) but trainable (the model can up-weight informative patches). The attention weights are interpretable — they yield free heatmap-style localisation of which patches drove the slide-level prediction. Every modern MIL variant (CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL, TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL, DSMIL, DTFD-MIL) descends from ABMIL.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
• Two-layer MLP over instance embeddings produces a scalar weight per instance.
  • Vanilla vs gated attention: gated multiplies the attention pre-activation by a separate sigmoid gate, which can improve calibration on harder bags.
  • Bag embedding = attention-weighted sum.
  • Classifier on top of the bag embedding.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• Sigmoid vs softmax attention?
  • Gated attention vs vanilla — gain depends on bag size and class boundary.
  • Attention temperature / scaling — affects heatmap sparsity.
  • Single-head vs multi-head for multi-class bags? (Multi-head leads to CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL-MB.)

docs.title: Representative article
docs.text: • ABMIL (Ilse, Tomczak, Welling 2018) — Ilse, Tomczak, Welling, ICML 2018.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Permutation-invariant — ignores patch positions in the slide. Spatial structure must come from elsewhere.
  • No instance-instance interaction — each instance is scored in isolation. TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL addresses this.
  • Single-class attention — multi-class extensions (CLAM-MB) need per-class branches.

docs.title: CellViT — Vision Transformers for Precise Cell Segmentation and Classification
docs.text:
stage: deep_wsi_learning · parents: —

Combine a SAM-pretrained (or DINOv2-pretrained) Vision Transformer backbone with a HoVer-Net-style three-decoder head (nuclear pixel + HV distance map + nuclear type). The ViT encoder provides richer, less stain-sensitive features than the original HoVer-Net CNN backbone, particularly when initialised from large-scale natural-image SSL (SAM, DINOv2). The decoder structure preserves HoVer-Net's instance-separation trick. CellViT outperforms HoVer-Net on PanNuke and is currently a strong open-source baseline for H&E cell segmentation + classification.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: HoVer-Net — Joint Nuclei Seg + Classification uses a CNN encoder (Pre-Act ResNet) that's now substantially weaker than a SAM- or DINOv2-pretrained ViT. CellViT keeps HoVer-Net's clever HV-decoder instance-separation trick — which still works — and upgrades only the encoder to a SAM-pretrained ViT-B or ViT-H. The richer encoder features substantially improve PanNuke nuclei segmentation and classification while preserving HoVer-Net's interpretable decoder structure.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
H&E patch → SAM-pretrained ViT-B / ViT-H encoder
   ↓
   → NP decoder  (nuclear pixel mask)
   → HV decoder  (horizontal-vertical distance maps)
   → NT decoder  (nuclear type)
post-processing: same watershed-style instance separation as HoVer-Net

The contribution is the encoder swap + careful adaptation of the ViT output to the three HoVer-Net decoder heads.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch (CellViT-256 takes 256×256; CellViT-SAM-H takes 1024×1024).
  • Output: per-pixel instance ID + per-nucleus class label.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• PanNuke — Pan-Cancer Nuclei Seg & Classification — primary benchmark.
  • Metrics: PQ, Dice, F1.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Larger model than HoVer-Net — slower training and inference.
  • Heavy reliance on SAM pretraining — when SAM weights are unavailable, CellViT loses its advantage over HoVer-Net.
  • PanNuke-only primary evaluation — multi-dataset generalisation less extensively validated than HoVer-Net's original claim.
  • Inference at WSI scale requires tiling and is slower than the CNN baseline.

docs.title: CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention Multi-Instance Learning
docs.text:
stage: deep_wsi_learning · parents: abmil

Extend ABMIL with (1) a single-branch (CLAM-SB) or multi-branch (CLAM-MB) class-specific attention head per class, and (2) an instance-level clustering loss that uses the highest- and lowest-attended patches as positive / negative pseudo-labels for an auxiliary classifier. The clustering signal regularises attention and substantially improves data efficiency on smaller cohorts. CLAM is the de-facto standard MIL baseline for pathology PFM evaluation in 2021–2025 thanks to its open-source repo and reliable attention heatmaps.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
CLAM is the standard open-source MIL aggregator in modern pathology (2021–2025). When a benchmark paper says "we evaluate UNI / GigaPath / Virchow with the standard MIL head", that head is almost always CLAM. Two reasons:

  1. Toolkit quality — mahmoodlab/CLAM ships an end-to-end pipeline: tissue segmentation, patch extraction, feature extraction (any backbone), MIL training, attention heatmap generation. It works.
  2. Reliable accuracy — CLAM matches or beats more recent aggregators on most pathology benchmarks while being simpler and faster than TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
CLAM extends ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning with two ideas:

  1. Per-class attention branches (CLAM-MB): instead of one attention map, learn one per class. Each branch produces its own bag embedding and class-specific score. CLAM-SB (single-branch) keeps one attention map and a slide-level softmax.
  2. Instance-level clustering loss: the highest-attended patches per class are treated as positive pseudo-labels and the lowest-attended patches as negative, training an auxiliary classifier on these. This regularises attention and improves data efficiency in low-slide-count regimes.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• SB vs MB: SB is simpler and often adequate for binary tasks; MB is preferred for ≥3 classes where per-class attention matters for interpretability.
  • Instance-loss weight: clinically meaningful when slides are heterogeneous (one tumour region in a large benign slide); can hurt when tumour fills most of the slide.
  • Backbone choice: ImageNet ResNet-50 (original) is now substantially weaker than UNI / GigaPath / Virchow / CTransPath — most of the modern accuracy gain over the original paper comes from upgrading the backbone, not the aggregator.

docs.title: Representative article
docs.text: • CLAM (Lu et al. 2021, Nat Biomed Eng) — Lu, Williamson, Chen et al., Nature Biomedical Engineering 5:555–570 (2021).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Permutation-invariant attention — ignores spatial layout. For spatial reasoning, use TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL or graph MIL.
  • Pseudo-labels from attention can be noisy in tumour-rich slides where top-attended and bottom-attended patches both contain tumour.
  • Original backbone is dated — pair with a modern PFM encoder.

docs.title: HoVer-Net — Joint Nuclei Instance Segmentation and Classification
docs.text:
stage: traditional_cpath, deep_wsi_learning · parents: —

CNN with three decoders applied to H&E patches: (1) nuclear pixel (NP) decoder producing a binary nuclei mask, (2) horizontal-vertical (HV) distance map decoder predicting per-pixel distance from each nucleus centre, used to split touching nuclei via watershed-style instance separation, and (3) nuclear type (NT) decoder producing a per-nucleus class label. Together they solve nuclei instance segmentation and classification in one forward pass. HoVer-Net is the canonical baseline for nuclei tasks in H&E pathology.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Before HoVer-Net, nuclei instance segmentation on H&E required either heavy multi-stage pipelines or struggled with touching nuclei — adjacent cells in dense tissue collapse into a single connected component. HoVer-Net solves this in one forward pass with three decoder branches whose outputs jointly determine instance masks and class labels. The horizontal-vertical (HV) distance map trick has since been adopted by CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification and many follow-ups, making HoVer-Net the canonical reference architecture for cell-level H&E analysis.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
H&E patch → CNN encoder (Pre-Act ResNet)
   ↓
   → NP decoder  (nuclear pixel mask — binary)
   → HV decoder  (per-pixel distance to nearest nucleus centre in x and y)
   → NT decoder  (nuclear type — per-nucleus class)
post-processing:
   - watershed-style instance separation using HV gradient + NP mask
   - assign each instance the dominant class from NT

The HV gradient acts as a learned instance-separation signal: where two touching nuclei meet, the HV map shows a sharp sign change in both x and y, which the watershed exploits.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
• Input: H&E patch (typically 256×256 at 40×).
  • Output: per-pixel instance ID + per-nucleus class label.

docs.title: Datasets / tasks / metrics
docs.text:
• PanNuke — Pan-Cancer Nuclei Seg & Classification — modern pan-cancer 5-class benchmark.
  • CoNSeP, Kumar, CPM — older datasets used in the original paper.
  • Metrics: PQ (Panoptic Quality), Dice, AJI, F1.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Multi-task loss balancing is sensitive — the paper provides ratios but ad-hoc cohorts need re-tuning.
  • Watershed post-processing is the main inference bottleneck at WSI scale.
  • CNN backbone is dated — CellViT — ViT Cell Segmentation + Classification replaces it with a SAM-pretrained ViT.
  • H&E only — IHC / IF need re-training.

docs.title: Patch-Level Self-Supervised Learning (Pathology)
docs.text:
stage: pathology_foundation_model · parents: pathology-foundation-model

Pretrain a patch-level visual encoder on millions of pathology image patches using self-supervised objectives — contrastive (MoCo, SimCLR), masked image modelling (MAE, MIM), or self-distillation (DINO, DINOv2) — *without* slide- level or pixel-level labels. The result is a general-purpose patch encoder that downstream slide-level pipelines (MIL aggregators, retrieval, anomaly detection) use as a frozen backbone. Patch-level SSL is the dominant pretraining strategy for modern pathology foundation models (CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit-DINO, UNI, Virchow, H-Optimus).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Pathology has too many unlabelled WSIs and too few labelled ones. Patch-level SSL inverts that asymmetry: pretrain a patch encoder on millions of unlabelled patches with a self-supervised objective, then transfer to downstream tasks via frozen features + lightweight heads (typically a MIL aggregator). This is the dominant pretraining recipe for the modern pathology foundation-model cohort: CTransPath (Swin-T, SRCL), Phikon, Lunit-DINO, UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2), Virchow, H-Optimus, PathDINO all sit here.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
millions of unlabelled H&E patches
   → encoder (ViT / Swin) with SSL objective (contrastive / DINO / MIM)
   → frozen patch encoder
   → downstream MIL aggregator on slide-level tasks

The downstream value comes from the encoder. Modern pipelines almost always freeze the SSL-pretrained encoder and train only the aggregator + classifier on top.

docs.title: Family of objectives
docs.text: Objective Example models Contrastive (MoCo / SimCLR) CTransPath (Swin-T, SRCL) (SRCL = MoCo v3 variant) iBOT (online distillation + MIM) Phikon DINO (self-distillation) Lunit-DINO DINOv2 (DINO + iBOT + KoLeo) UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2), Virchow, H-Optimus Masked Image Modelling (MAE) (less common in pathology so far)

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• Which SSL objective transfers best to pathology — contrastive vs DINO vs MIM?
  • How much pretraining data is enough — TCGA-only vs multi-cohort millions?
  • What patch size / magnification mix maximises downstream utility?
  • How do gains scale with model size and pretraining compute?
  • How does patch-level SSL compare against slide-level pretraining (GigaPath)?

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Frozen-feature ceiling — for a given downstream task, end-to-end fine-tuning of a small specialist model can sometimes outperform frozen PFM features.
  • Pretraining stain bias — TCGA-only pretraining underperforms on non-TCGA stains; multi-cohort pretraining is needed for robust generalisation.
  • No language alignment — pure patch-level SSL gives no zero-shot capability; need a separate VL alignment step (CONCH / MUSK / PLIP).

docs.text:

When the user asks "which PFM encoder should I use?", default to UNI (DINOv2 ViT-L) for the strongest current frozen features, CTransPath for an open-weights compute-cheap baseline. Cite this method node when discussing pretraining strategies in the abstract.

docs.title: Pathology Vision-Language Models
docs.text:
stage: pathology_vlm · parents: —

Align pathology image features with text descriptions (captions, reports, textbook excerpts) via large-scale image-text contrastive pretraining (CLIP-style) or generative alignment (caption / report generation), to enable zero-shot classification, retrieval, and natural-language querying of histopathology images. The text encoder serves as a flexible classifier whose label set can change at inference time, sidestepping per-task fine-tuning. Pathology VLMs are the foundational technology under modern pathology MLLMs (PathChat, PathGen, MUSK) and zero-shot WSI pipelines (MI-Zero, CONCH-MIL).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most pathology classification pipelines require per-task fine-tuning with labelled slides. Pathology VL models replace the per-task classifier head with a text encoder: candidate class names become text prompts, the model picks the closest text to the image embedding. The class set can change at inference time without retraining — a step-change in flexibility for diagnostic pipelines that need many fine-grained labels.

Pathology VL models also enable:

  • Image-text retrieval — find similar histology + similar reports for case review.
  • Histology captioning — generate natural-language descriptions of patches.
  • Pathology VQA — natural-language questions about images.
  • Retrieval-augmented reasoning — feed retrieved similar cases into a downstream MLLM.

Modern pathology MLLMs (PathChat, MUSK, PathGen) all build on a VL foundation; without it, an MLLM cannot ground its language in pathology image semantics.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
H&E patch                pathology text (caption / report / textbook)
   ↓                                  ↓
image encoder                    text encoder
   ↓                                  ↓
projection → joint embedding space ← projection
   ↓
contrastive InfoNCE loss: matched pairs close, mismatched far

After training, zero-shot classification is:

prob(class | image) ∝ exp(<image_emb, text_emb(prompt(class))>)

docs.title: Family of sub-approaches
docs.text: Sub-branch Examples Image-text contrastive (CLIP-style) PLIP, CONCH, QuiltNet, MUSK Report alignment many recent biomedical VL models Histology captioning ARCH, PathGen-LLaVA Pathology VQA PathChat, PathVQA, Quilt-LLaVA Retrieval-augmented reasoning RAG-PathChat-style pipelines Slide-level VL (MIL on VL features) MI-Zero (Lu et al. 2023, CVPR), CONCH-MIL

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• Where does the text come from — captions, reports, Twitter, textbooks?
  • Image-text contrastive (CLIP) vs generative captioning vs instruction-tuned MLLM?
  • How does zero-shot accuracy compare against frozen-feature linear probing?
  • How to extend patch-level VL alignment to slide-level (MI-Zero, CONCH-MIL)?
  • What text vocabulary covers diagnostic pathology adequately?

docs.title: Representative articles
docs.text:
• CLIP (Radford et al. 2021, ICML) — the foundational dual-encoder contrastive recipe.
  • PLIP (Huang et al. 2023, Nat Med) — first widely-cited pathology VL, from Twitter-mined OpenPath.
  • MI-Zero (Lu et al. 2023, CVPR) — patch-VL extended to slide-level zero-shot via top-k aggregation.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Text supervision quality varies — Twitter captions are noisy; clinical reports are gold but hard to obtain at scale.
  • Prompt engineering still matters — small prompt changes shift zero-shot accuracy.
  • Zero-shot lags supervised for most tasks; useful in label-poor regimes but not always SOTA.
  • Patch-level only in early VL models — slide-level needs additional aggregation (MI-Zero) or slide-level pretraining (CONCH-MIL).

docs.title: TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated Multiple Instance Learning
docs.text:
stage: deep_wsi_learning · parents: weakly-supervised-mil

Replace ABMIL's MLP-attention aggregator with a Transformer encoder that models instance-instance correlations. Two ingredients: (1) a Nyström-based attention approximation to make self-attention feasible on bags of thousands of patches; (2) a Pyramid Position Encoding Generator (PPEG) to re-inject 2-D spatial context into the sequence. The result captures correlations between distant patches that mean / attention pooling cannot.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning and CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL treat patches as independent instances — the attention score for one patch does not depend on what the others contain. In pathology, that assumption breaks: tumour regions are spatially contiguous, immune infiltration is contextual, gland architecture only makes sense across multiple patches. TransMIL fixes this with Transformer self-attention, which lets every patch attend to every other patch. To make this tractable on bags of thousands of patches it uses:

  • Nyström attention approximation — drops attention cost from O(N²) to O(N).
  • Pyramid Position Encoding Generator (PPEG) — re-injects 2-D spatial context into the otherwise permutation-invariant Transformer sequence via multi-scale convolutions on the bag.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
patches → linear proj → [CLS] + sequence
   → PPEG (spatial conv)
   → Nyström-attention Transformer layers
   → take [CLS] embedding → classifier

The Transformer captures distant-patch correlations that attention pooling cannot. PPEG restores enough spatial signal that the model can reason about tissue architecture.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• Nyström vs exact attention: Nyström is an approximation; on small bags, exact attention can outperform.
  • Number of Transformer layers / heads: original paper uses 2 layers; deeper helps marginally and costs compute.
  • Does PPEG matter? Ablations in the paper show it does — random 2-D mixing alone underperforms.
  • Backbone interaction: as with other MIL methods, the patch encoder choice (ImageNet vs CTransPath vs UNI) dominates accuracy gains.

docs.title: Representative article
docs.text: • TransMIL (Shao et al. 2021, NeurIPS) — Shao et al., NeurIPS 2021.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Approximate attention — Nyström adds variance; exact attention on small bags can do better.
  • Parameter cost — adds Transformer parameters vs ABMIL/CLAM; compute-bound deployment may prefer simpler aggregators.
  • Less interpretable than CLAM's per-class attention branches — visualising "what the Transformer attends to" is non-trivial.

docs.title: How Claude should use this method
docs.text:
skill · methods

Reach for TransMIL when instance-instance correlations matter (survival, complex subtyping, spatial architectural cues). For most binary slide-level classification, CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL is simpler and adequate.

docs.title: Weakly-Supervised Multiple Instance Learning (WSI)
docs.text:
stage: deep_wsi_learning · parents: —

Treat a whole-slide image as a bag of patch instances and train end-to-end with only a slide-level label, without per-patch annotation. The aggregator (mean / max → attention → transformer → graph) learns to weigh patch contributions to the slide prediction. WSI MIL is the dominant paradigm for any slide-level classification task in pathology and the immediate predecessor of pathology foundation models — most modern PFM pipelines still use an MIL aggregator on top of frozen PFM features.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Slide-level labels are cheap (extracted from clinical reports). Patch-level labels are expensive (pathologist time at >1 GPx scale per slide). Weakly-supervised MIL closes that gap: treat each WSI as a bag of patch instances, supervise only at bag level, and let the aggregator learn which patches drive the prediction. WSI MIL is the dominant paradigm for any slide-level classification task in pathology — and the immediate precursor of pathology foundation models, most of which still use a MIL aggregator on top of frozen PFM features.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
A typical pipeline:

  1. Tile the WSI into thousands of fixed-size patches at a chosen magnification.
  2. Encode each patch with a backbone (ImageNet ViT, CTransPath, UNI, GigaPath, Virchow).
  3. Aggregate patch features into a single bag-level vector. Aggregator choices:
  4. mean / max pool (parametric-free)
  5. learned attention (ABMIL — Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning)
  6. per-class attention with instance clustering (CLAM — Clustering-constrained Attention MIL)
  7. Transformer self-attention (TransMIL — Transformer-based Correlated MIL)
  8. graph neural networks (cell / tissue graphs)
  9. Classify the bag vector.
  10. Visualise the attention map for free localisation.

docs.title: Key questions
docs.text:
• How to aggregate thousands of patches into one slide prediction?
  • How to make attention spatially interpretable for clinician-facing heatmaps?
  • How to scale beyond memory: gradient checkpointing, foreground sampling, hierarchical aggregation?
  • How to handle weak / noisy slide labels (report mining)?
  • When to fine-tune the encoder end-to-end vs use frozen PFM features?

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
• Tumour detection (Camelyon16 — Cancer Metastases in Lymph Nodes 2016)
  • Slide-level subtype classification (TCGA-NSCLC, TCGA-RCC)
  • Grading (PANDA — Prostate cANcer graDe Assessment)
  • Survival prediction
  • Biomarker / mutation prediction from H&E

docs.title: Representative articles
docs.text:
• ABMIL (Ilse, Tomczak, Welling 2018) — the foundational attention aggregator
  • CLAM (Lu et al. 2021, Nat Biomed Eng) — the de-facto modern open-source MIL toolkit
  • TransMIL (Shao et al. 2021, NeurIPS) — Transformer aggregation with correlation modelling
  • Campanella et al. 2019 — Clinical-Grade Weakly-Supervised Pathology MIL — clinical-grade scale demonstration (~44k MSKCC slides)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Bag-of-patches loses fine spatial structure unless explicit position encoding (TransMIL) or graphs are used.
  • Long-tail aggregators: most attention is on a few patches, the rest are essentially ignored.
  • Backbone quality dominates: ImageNet ResNet-50 features are now substantially weaker than UNI / GigaPath; aggregator gains are smaller than backbone gains.
  • Heatmaps are correlative, not causal — clinical interpretation requires care.

docs.title: CTransPath
docs.text: Swin Transformer Tiny (modified) · ~28M · weights open · Tencent AI Lab (Wang et al.) github · doi

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2), GigaPath, and Virchow, CTransPath was the strongest open-source pathology SSL checkpoint. Released by Tencent AI Lab in 2022, it brought transformer pretraining on TCGA-scale pathology data into the open-source toolchain and was the de-facto patch encoder for many WSI MIL pipelines through 2023–2024.

Today it remains useful as:

  • The open-weights compute-cheap baseline when UNI's gated weights are unavailable or compute is tight.
  • The pre-UNI predecessor to cite when documenting the evolution of pathology PFMs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Backbone: Swin Transformer Tiny (~28M parameters, modified for SSL).
  • Input: H&E patches at 224×224.
  • Output: 768-dim patch embeddings (verify against the repo).

docs.title: Pretraining
docs.text:
• Objective: SRCL — Semantically-Relevant Contrastive Learning, a MoCo v3 variant that augments standard contrastive pairs with semantically-related positives drawn from a learned memory bank.
  • Data: ~32k WSIs from TCGA + PAIP, ~15M H&E patches.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• H&E patch encoding (vision only) for downstream classification / MIL / retrieval.
  • Drop-in replacement for ImageNet-pretrained CNNs in any pathology pipeline.
  • Open weights — no gating, easy reproduction.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Smaller backbone (~28M params) than modern PFMs (UNI ViT-L ~307M, Virchow ViT-H ~632M).
  • Limited pretraining cohort (TCGA + PAIP) — less stain diversity than 100k+ WSI PFMs.
  • Embedding dim 768 vs UNI's 1024 — small representation cost downstream.
  • No vision-language alignment.

docs.title: How Claude should use this model
docs.text:
skill · models

Pick CTransPath when:

  • Open weights matter and gated PFMs (UNI, Virchow) are off-limits.
  • Compute budget is tight and a smaller backbone is acceptable.
  • Documenting the pre-UNI baseline for a comparison table.

Pick UNI (ViT-L/16, DINOv2) when the strongest possible H&E encoder is needed.
